idea: In select(), (1) drop exact duplicates by hashing the whitespace-normalized, lowercased text, and drop junk documents whose share of non-ASCII characters exceeds 5% or that contain spam phrases such as "Click here" or "Order ... online". (2) Fit a sklearn TfidfVectorizer (word unigrams and bigrams, sublinear_tf=True) on target_sample, score each remaining doc by cosine similarity to the mean target vector, and sort by score descending. (3) Walk that sorted list, counting tokens with tiktoken "gpt2", and keep docs until the running total reaches T; return those indices in that order, so the trainer never needs to cycle.
why: The pool is about half off-domain spam, code, and forum junk, while the target is Wikipedia-style articles, so filtering out junk and putting the documents most similar to the target first should lower held-out bpb below the random-shuffle baseline of 1.9636.
outcome: dev 1.9675 against 1.9636 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: In select(), split the pool into two groups by a format test and keep the random seeded shuffle within each group. Group A ("wiki-format") is every doc that starts with a "= Title =" heading line (regex ^= .+ =\s*\n) and contains the token " @-@ " or at least 5 occurrences of " , " ; everything else is group B. Drop any doc that matches the junk rules (contains "Click here", "discount code", "coupon", or has more than 5% non-ASCII characters) and drop exact duplicates by whitespace-normalized lowercased hash. Return all of group A (shuffled with random.Random(CURATE_SEED)) followed by all of group B (shuffled the same way). Do not use TF-IDF or any similarity ranking, and do not truncate: the trainer's own cycling handles the length. Ordering by format is a yes/no split, so it can't reorder documents by their similarity to the target the way the rejected cosine ranking did.
why: The target sample is Wikipedia articles in a specific tokenized style (" @-@ ", spaced punctuation, "= Title =" headings), and the pool contains many docs in that same format, so putting them first should move the early training tokens toward the target distribution while keeping the rest of the data in random order instead of ranking it by cosine similarity, which was the part that hurt.
outcome: dev 2.1001 against 1.9636 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: In select(), keep the original seeded random shuffle of the whole pool, but first remove junk and duplicates without reordering anything. Drop a doc if its whitespace-normalized, lowercased text hash was already seen (keep the first occurrence). Drop a doc if more than 5% of its characters are non-ASCII, or if it contains "Click here", "discount code", or "coupon". Then shuffle the surviving indices with random.Random(int(os.environ.get("CURATE_SEED", 0))) and return them. Do not use TF-IDF, similarity to target_sample, format grouping, or truncation, so the trainer still reads the list front to back and cycles if needed.
why: The first experiment combined junk filtering with TF-IDF ranking and the second reordered by format, so neither isolates whether filtering alone helps; a filter-only change that keeps the random order tests that cleanly against the 1.9636 baseline.
outcome: dev 2.0258 against 1.9636 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: In select(), keep the original seeded random shuffle of the whole pool, and drop only obvious SEO spam: remove a doc if it contains "Click here" AND ("save 70%" or "Limited offer"), using plain substring checks on the raw text. Do not apply the non-ASCII share rule, the "coupon" or "discount code" rules, duplicate hashing, TF-IDF, format grouping, or truncation. Shuffle the surviving indices with random.Random(int(os.environ.get("CURATE_SEED", 0))) and return them, so the trainer still cycles if needed.
why: Experiment 3 lost about 0.06 bpb, and its 5% non-ASCII rule probably discarded in-domain Wikipedia text, since the target uses en dashes and "@-@" tokens, so a narrower filter that removes only clear spam should isolate whether junk removal helps at all.
outcome: dev 2.0104 against 1.9636 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: In select(), keep the seeded random shuffle within two groups, but reverse the group order from experiment 2 and fix the length. Group A is every doc that starts with a "= Title =" heading line (regex ^= .+ =\s*\n) or contains " @-@ ", as in experiment 2. Group B is everything else. Do no junk filtering, deduplication, TF-IDF, or similarity ranking. Shuffle each group with random.Random(int(os.environ.get("CURATE_SEED", 0))). Build the output as a prefix of shuffled B followed by all of shuffled A, so the final segment the trainer reads is wiki-format. Choose the B prefix so the total is exactly T tokens, counting with tiktoken "gpt2". If A alone exceeds T, keep only the last T tokens of A. Return the indices in that order so the trainer does not need to cycle.
why: Experiment 2 put wiki-format docs first and non-wiki docs last, and dev bpb got much worse (2.10 vs 1.96), which suggests the data seen last in training matters a lot; reversing that order tests whether ending on target-style text helps, and it avoids the rejected ranking and filtering steps.
outcome: dev 1.9032 against 1.9636 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea: Keep the experiment-5 structure exactly (seeded shuffle of group B as a token-counted prefix, then all of group A last, total exactly T tokens), but reorder group A before concatenation: fit a sklearn TfidfVectorizer (word unigrams and bigrams, sublinear_tf=True) on target_sample, compute each group-A doc's cosine similarity to the mean target vector, and sort group A ascending by that score so the most target-like wiki-format docs come last. Leave group B's seeded shuffle, the B-prefix token budget, and the no-junk-filtering and no-dedup rules unchanged. Only the order inside the final segment changes.
why: The biggest gain so far came from moving wiki-format text to the end of the stream, which suggests the last-read in-domain tokens dominate the held-out bpb, so ordering within that final segment by similarity to the target may help further; this avoids the earlier rejected cosine ranking of the whole pool, which mixed in off-domain docs.
outcome: dev 1.9121 against 1.9032 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep the experiment-5 structure exactly (seeded shuffle of group B as a token-counted prefix, then all of group A last, total exactly T tokens, no junk filtering, no dedup, no TF-IDF). Change only the group A membership test. A doc goes to group A if it matches the heading regex ^= .+ =\s*\n, OR contains " @-@ ", OR contains " @,@ " or " @.@ ", OR has at least 5 occurrences of " , " together with at least 5 occurrences of " . ". Everything else goes to group B. Shuffle each group with random.Random(int(os.environ.get("CURATE_SEED", 0))) as before, and keep the B-prefix token budget and the A-alone-exceeds-T fallback unchanged.
why: The gain in experiment 5 came from ending the training stream with WikiText-style tokenized text, and the target sample is that style, so widening group A to catch more wiki-format docs without a heading or " @-@ " (via the " @,@ "/" @.@ " markers and the " , "/" . " spacing signature) should put more in-domain text in that final segment without changing the ordering logic that has already worked.
outcome: dev 1.9029 against 1.9032 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep the experiment-5 structure (seeded shuffle of group B as a token-counted prefix, then group A last, total exactly T tokens, no junk filtering, no dedup, no TF-IDF), but upsample group A by repeating it. Build A1 = shuffled group A and A2 = a second, independently reseeded shuffle of group A (random.Random(seed + 1)). Form the tail as A1 + A2 and count its tokens with tiktoken "gpt2". Choose the B prefix so that B-prefix tokens + len(A1 + A2) = T exactly, which means the B prefix shrinks as the A tail grows. If A1 + A2 alone exceeds T, keep the last T tokens of A1 + A2 (whole documents, as in the existing fallback). Return the indices in that order so the trainer does not need to cycle.
why: The held-out target is wiki-format text and the trainer reads the final segment last, so doubling the wiki-format tail should shift more of the 9.8M-token budget toward target-like data without changing the total length, which should lower dev bpb relative to the single-copy version (1.9032). This is a different lever from the rejected changes: it changes the amount of group A rather than its filtering or its internal ordering.
outcome: dev 1.9374 against 1.9032 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep experiment 5 exactly, including the seeded shuffle of group B, the token-counted B prefix, and group A last. Change only the order of the B prefix: after choosing the prefix as the first N shuffled group-B docs that fill the token budget, sort those prefix docs ascending by cosine similarity to the mean target TF-IDF vector (sklearn TfidfVectorizer, word unigrams and bigrams, sublinear_tf=True, fit on target_sample), so the most target-like B docs sit immediately before group A. Do not filter junk, dedupe, or change which docs are in the prefix or the total token count.
why: The prefix membership stays the same as the current best, so any change in dev bpb comes from ordering alone. Ordering by similarity inside group A (experiment 6) was slightly worse, but placing the most target-like general text just before the wiki segment is untested and could help the model's final adaptation to the target domain.
outcome: dev 2.0220 against 1.9032 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep experiment 5 exactly (seeded shuffle of group B as a token-counted prefix, then all of group A last, total exactly T tokens, no junk filtering, no TF-IDF), and add one change: drop exact duplicates before anything else. Hash each doc by its whitespace-normalized, lowercased text and keep only the first occurrence, preserving pool order. Then run the existing group split, seeded shuffles (random.Random(int(os.environ.get("CURATE_SEED", 0)))), B-prefix token budget, and A-alone-exceeds-T fallback on the deduplicated list. No other filter is applied.
why: Duplicates spend the fixed T-token budget on repeated text, so removing them lets the B prefix include more unique documents, and this isolates dedup from the junk filters that were bundled into experiment 3 and hurt results.
outcome: dev 1.9056 against 1.9032 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep experiment 5 exactly (group A = heading or " @-@ " docs placed last, group B seeded-shuffled and filled as a token-counted prefix to total exactly T), but apply junk filtering to group B only, before the shuffle. Drop any group-B doc that contains "Click here", "discount code", "coupon", or matches the pattern "Order .* online" (case-insensitive), or whose share of non-ASCII characters exceeds 5%. Leave group A completely unfiltered and undeduplicated, and keep the same random.Random(int(os.environ.get("CURATE_SEED", 0))) shuffle and the same token-counted B-prefix budget, so the prefix simply draws from the cleaned B list.
why: Experiment 5 wins because the wiki-format tail sits last, but the bulk of the T-token budget comes from group B, which still contains the SEO spam and damaged text seen in the pool sample; removing that junk only from the B prefix should cut noise in most of the training tokens without touching the wiki-format segment that earlier junk filters (which were applied across the whole pool and in other structures) may have disturbed.
outcome: dev 2.0486 against 1.9032 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep experiment 5 exactly (group A = heading or " @-@ " docs placed last, group B seeded-shuffled and filled as a token-counted prefix to total exactly T), but drop source-code documents from group B before the shuffle. A group-B doc counts as code if at least 3 of its lines match the regex ^\s*(from \S+ import |import \S+|def |class |#include|return |if __name__) (multiline). Do not apply the non-ASCII, "Click here", coupon, or dedup rules, and leave group A untouched.
why: Source code is a clearly off-domain block in the pool, and a narrow code-only removal targets it without the broad junk rules that hurt in experiments 1, 3, 4 and 11, which likely also discarded wiki text that contains non-ASCII characters such as en dashes.
outcome: dev 1.9163 against 1.9032 for the best at the time, rejected
